declarations.statement:
lemma smul_eq_zero_iff'' [AddMonoid M] (f : α → α → M) :
    (∀ i j : α, δ[i,j] • f i j = 0) ↔ ∀ i : α, f i i = 0

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.symm
declarations.statement: lemma symm (i j : α) : δ[i,j] = δ[j,i]

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.smul_symm
declarations.statement: lemma smul_symm [AddMonoid M] (i j : α) (f : α → α → M) : δ[i,j] • f j i = δ[i,j] • f i j

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.symmetrize
declarations.statement:
lemma symmetrize [AddMonoid M] (i j : α) (f : α → α → M) :
    δ[i,j] • (f i j + f j i) = (2 * δ[i,j]) • f i j

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.symmetrize'
declarations.statement:
lemma symmetrize' [AddCommMonoid M] {K : Type*} [Semifield K] [CharZero K] [Module K M]
    (i j : α) (f : α → α → M) : δ[i,j] • (2 : K)⁻¹ • (f i j + f j i) = δ[i,j] • f i j

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.smul_sub_eq_zero
declarations.statement: lemma smul_sub_eq_zero [AddGroup M] (i j : α) (f : α → α → M) : δ[i,j] • (f i j - f j i) = 0

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.sum_mul
declarations.statement: lemma sum_mul [Fintype α] (i j : α) : ∑ k : α, δ[i,k] * δ[k,j] = δ[i,j]

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.sum_smul
declarations.statement: lemma sum_smul [Fintype α] (i : α) (f : α → M) : ∑ j : α, δ[i,j] • f j = f i

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.sum_sum_smul_eq_zero
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_sum_smul_eq_zero [Fintype α] {f : α → α → M} (hf : ∀ i : α, f i i = 0) :
    ∑ i : α, ∑ j : α, δ[i,j] • f i j = 0

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.finset_sum_smul
declarations.statement:
lemma finset_sum_smul (s : Finset α) (i : α) (f : α → M) :
    ∑ j ∈ s, δ[i,j] • f j = if i ∈ s then f i else 0

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.finset_sum_sum_smul_eq_zero
declarations.statement:
lemma finset_sum_sum_smul_eq_zero {s s' : Finset α} {f : α → α → M}
    (hf : ∀ i ∈ s ∩ s', f i i = 0) : ∑ i ∈ s, ∑ j ∈ s', δ[i,j] • f i j = 0

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.generalizedKroneckerDelta
declarations.doc:
Generalized Kronecker delta:
`δ^{μ₁...μₙ}_{ν₁...νₙ} = det (δ[μᵢ, νⱼ])`.

This is defined for any finite type `α` with decidable equality.
declarations.statement:
def generalizedKroneckerDelta {α ι : Type} [DecidableEq α]
    [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype ι]
    (μ : ι → α) (ν : ι → α) : ℤ

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.generalizedKroneckerDelta_swap
declarations.doc:
Swapping two of the upper indices of the generalized Kronecker delta negates it.
This is one row transposition of the underlying determinant.
declarations.statement:
lemma generalizedKroneckerDelta_swap {α ι : Type} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype ι]
    (μ ν : ι → α) {i j : ι} (hij : i ≠ j) :
    generalizedKroneckerDelta (μ ∘ Equiv.swap i j) ν = - generalizedKroneckerDelta μ ν

declarations.name: KroneckerDelta.generalizedKroneckerDelta_comp_perm
declarations.doc:
Simultaneously reindexing the upper and lower slots of a generalized Kronecker delta by the
same permutation leaves it unchanged.
declarations.statement:
lemma generalizedKroneckerDelta_comp_perm {α ι : Type} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq ι]
    [Fintype ι] (μ ν : ι → α) (e : Equiv.Perm ι) :
    generalizedKroneckerDelta (μ ∘ e) (ν ∘ e) = generalizedKroneckerDelta μ ν

modules.title: Contraction identities for the generalized Kronecker delta
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

This file proves the combinatorial contraction facts for the `generalizedKroneckerDelta`
(defined in `Physlib.Mathematics.KroneckerDelta.Basic`). Everything here is purely about the
abstract generalized Kronecker delta on a finite type; no tensor or physics content appears.
These facts are the reusable backbone of the Levi-Civita epsilon-epsilon contraction
identities proved in `Physlib.Relativity.Tensors.LeviCivita.Contractions`.

The central fact is that summing a `generalizedKroneckerDelta` over one shared index lowers
its rank by one and multiplies it by `card α - n` (`generalizedKroneckerDelta_sum_snoc`).
Iterating that fact gives the fully-, singly-, and doubly-free contractions over an arbitrary
finite index type, with the falling product `(card α - m) (card α - m - 1) ⋯` for `m` free pairs
(`sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_card`, `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons_card`,
`sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂_card`), and `k!` for the full contraction when the index type
has `k` elements (`sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_eq_factorial`). Together with the product
identity
`generalizedKroneckerDelta μ ν = generalizedKroneckerDelta μ id * generalizedKroneckerDelta ν id`
(`generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul`), their `Fin 4` instances `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self`,
`sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons`, and `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂` give the
contractions used for the Levi-Civita identities.

The proof of `generalizedKroneckerDelta_sum_snoc` borders the delta matrix with the appended
index (a Schur-complement reduction) and then applies the ring-general rank-one determinant
update lemma `Matrix.det_add_rankOne`, which is proved here because Mathlib only provides the
matrix determinant lemma when `det A` is a unit and Kronecker-delta matrices are singular.

## ii. Key results

- `generalizedKroneckerDelta_sum_snoc` : summing over one shared index lowers the rank by one.
- `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_card`, `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons_card`,
  `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂_card` : the fully-, singly-, and doubly-free contractions
  over any finite index type; `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_eq_factorial` : the full
  contraction is `k!` when the type has `k` elements.
- `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_self`, `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons`,
  `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_snoc`, `sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons₂` : the
  fully-, singly-, and doubly-free symbol-level contractions over `Fin 4`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The rank-one determinant update
- B. Contraction identities

## iv. References

* None.

sections.text: ## A. The rank-one determinant update
## B. Contraction identities

declarations.name: generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul
declarations.doc:
The product of two Levi-Civita-type symbols is a generalized Kronecker delta:
`δ^{μ}_{·} · δ^{ν}_{·} = δ^{μ}_{ν}`, where each single factor is a Kronecker matrix against the
identity. This is the Lean form of `ε^{μ₁…μₙ} ε_{ν₁…νₙ} = δ^{μ₁…μₙ}_{ν₁…νₙ}`.
declarations.statement:
lemma generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul (μ ν : α → α) :
    generalizedKroneckerDelta μ id * generalizedKroneckerDelta ν id
      = generalizedKroneckerDelta μ ν

declarations.name: generalizedKroneckerDelta_sum_snoc
declarations.doc:
**Generalized Kronecker delta contraction.** Summing a `generalizedKroneckerDelta` over one
shared index appended at the end lowers the rank by one and pulls out a factor of `card α - n`.
This is the reusable combinatorial fact behind all epsilon-epsilon identities.
declarations.statement:
lemma generalizedKroneckerDelta_sum_snoc {n : ℕ} (μ ν : Fin n → α) :
    ∑ a : α, generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.snoc μ a) (Fin.snoc ν a)
      = ((Fintype.card α : ℤ) - n) * generalizedKroneckerDelta μ ν

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_card
declarations.doc:
**Full contraction over an arbitrary finite type.** Summing `δ^{h}_{h}` over all `k`-tuples
`h` of indices gives the falling product `card α · (card α - 1) ⋯ (card α - k + 1)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_card (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → α, generalizedKroneckerDelta h h
      = ∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((Fintype.card α : ℤ) - j)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons_card
declarations.doc:
**Single contraction over an arbitrary finite type.** Contracting the last `k` of `k+1`
index pairs leaves one free pair `σ, τ`, with the falling product
`(card α - 1) (card α - 2) ⋯`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons_card (σ τ : α) (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → α,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons σ h) (Fin.cons τ h)
      = (∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((Fintype.card α : ℤ) - 1 - j))
        * ((kroneckerDelta σ τ : ℕ) : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂_card
declarations.doc:
**Double contraction over an arbitrary finite type.** Contracting the last `k` of `k+2`
index pairs leaves two free pairs, with value a `2×2` generalized Kronecker delta times the
falling product `(card α - 2) (card α - 3) ⋯`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂_card (ρ σ τ ω : α) (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → α,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons ρ (Fin.cons σ h)) (Fin.cons τ (Fin.cons ω h))
      = (∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((Fintype.card α : ℤ) - 2 - j))
        * generalizedKroneckerDelta ![ρ, σ] ![τ, ω]

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_eq_factorial
declarations.doc: When the index type has exactly `k` elements, the full contraction is `k!`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_eq_factorial {k : ℕ} (hk : Fintype.card α = k) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → α, generalizedKroneckerDelta h h = (k.factorial : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self
declarations.doc:
**Full contraction.** Iterating the snoc contraction over all four indices:
`∑_f δ^{f}_{f} = 4!`. Here `f` ranges over all maps `Fin 4 → Fin 4`. The `Fin 4` instance of
`sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self_card`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_self (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → Fin 4, generalizedKroneckerDelta h h
      = ∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((4 : ℤ) - j)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons
declarations.doc:
**Single contraction.** Contracting the last `k` of `k+1` index pairs leaves one free pair
`σ, τ`, with the factorial factor `(4-1)(4-2)…`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons (σ τ : Fin 4) (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → Fin 4,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons σ h) (Fin.cons τ h)
      = (∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((3 : ℤ) - j)) * ((kroneckerDelta σ τ : ℕ) : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂
declarations.doc:
**Double contraction.** Contracting the last `k` of `k+2` index pairs leaves two free pairs,
with value a `2×2` generalized Kronecker delta times the factorial factor.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_cons₂ (ρ σ τ ω : Fin 4) (k : ℕ) :
    ∑ h : Fin k → Fin 4,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons ρ (Fin.cons σ h)) (Fin.cons τ (Fin.cons ω h))
      = (∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, ((2 : ℤ) - j))
        * generalizedKroneckerDelta ![ρ, σ] ![τ, ω]

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_self
declarations.doc: Symbol-level full contraction over `Fin 4 → Fin 4`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_self :
    ∑ g : Fin 4 → Fin 4,
      generalizedKroneckerDelta g id * generalizedKroneckerDelta g id = (24 : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons
declarations.doc: Symbol-level triple contraction, one free pair `σ, τ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons (σ τ : Fin 4) :
    ∑ h : Fin 3 → Fin 4,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons σ h) id
          * generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons τ h) id
      = 6 * ((kroneckerDelta σ τ : ℕ) : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_snoc
declarations.doc: Symbol-level triple contraction with the free index in the last slot.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_snoc (σ τ : Fin 4) :
    ∑ h : Fin 3 → Fin 4,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.snoc h σ) id * generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.snoc h τ) id =
      6 * ((kroneckerDelta σ τ : ℕ) : ℤ)

declarations.name: sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons₂
declarations.doc: Symbol-level double contraction, two free pairs.
declarations.statement:
lemma sum_generalizedKroneckerDelta_mul_cons₂ (ρ σ τ ω : Fin 4) :
    ∑ h : Fin 2 → Fin 4,
        generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons ρ (Fin.cons σ h)) id
          * generalizedKroneckerDelta (Fin.cons τ (Fin.cons ω h)) id
      = 2 * (((kroneckerDelta ρ τ : ℕ) : ℤ) * ((kroneckerDelta σ ω : ℕ) : ℤ)
          - ((kroneckerDelta ρ ω : ℕ) : ℤ) * ((kroneckerDelta σ τ : ℕ) : ℤ))

modules.title: The Levi-Civita symbol in general dimension
modules.doc:
## i. Overview

This module defines the Levi-Civita symbol `leviCivitaSymbol` on a general finite index
type `ι`: for `g : ι → ι` it is the sign of `g` when `g` is a permutation and `0`
otherwise. Taking `ι = Fin d` gives the Levi-Civita symbol `ε_{i₁ ⋯ i_d}` in dimension
`d`, normalized by `ε_{0 1 ⋯ (d-1)} = 1`.

The definition is the `generalizedKroneckerDelta` of `g` against the identity, i.e. the
determinant of the matrix of Kronecker deltas `δ[g i, j]`, so the basic properties are
inherited from the determinant: the value `1` on the identity, antisymmetry under
transposition of two indices, vanishing on repeated indices, and the sign of a
permutation via `Matrix.det_permutation`.

## ii. Key results

- `leviCivitaSymbol` : the Levi-Civita symbol on a finite index type, valued in `ℤ`.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_id` : the normalization `ε_{0 1 ⋯ (d-1)} = 1`.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_perm` : on a permutation `σ` the symbol is the sign of `σ`.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_comp_swap` : antisymmetry under transposition of two indices.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_swap_comp` : antisymmetry under transposition of two index values.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_iff` : the symbol vanishes exactly on repeated indices.
- `leviCivitaSymbol_eq_prod_prod_Ioi` : on `Fin n` the symbol is the product over pairs
  `i < j` of the sign of `g j - g i`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Definition
- B. Value on permutations
- C. Antisymmetry
- D. Vanishing on repeated indices
- E. Closed form on `Fin n`

## iv. References

* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi-Civita_symbol. [ref: wiki_levi_civita_symbol]

sections.text: ## A. Definition
## B. Value on permutations
## C. Antisymmetry
## D. Vanishing on repeated indices
## E. Closed form on `Fin n`

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol on a finite index type `ι`: `leviCivitaSymbol g` is the sign
of `g` when `g : ι → ι` is a permutation, and `0` otherwise. It is the generalized
Kronecker delta of `g` against the identity, i.e. the determinant of the matrix of
Kronecker deltas `δ[g i, j]`.

For `ι = Fin d` this is the Levi-Civita symbol `ε_{i₁ ⋯ i_d}` in dimension `d`,
normalized by `ε_{0 1 ⋯ (d-1)} = 1`.
declarations.statement: def leviCivitaSymbol (g : ι → ι) : ℤ

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_eq_det
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol as the determinant of the matrix of Kronecker deltas
`δ[g i, j]`.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_eq_det (g : ι → ι) :
    leviCivitaSymbol g = Matrix.det (fun i j => ((kroneckerDelta (g i) j : ℕ) : ℤ))

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_id
declarations.doc: The Levi-Civita symbol of the identity, i.e. `ε_{0 1 ⋯ (d-1)}`, is `1`.
declarations.statement: lemma leviCivitaSymbol_id : leviCivitaSymbol (id : ι → ι) = 1

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_perm
declarations.doc: The Levi-Civita symbol of a permutation `σ` is the sign of `σ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_perm (σ : Equiv.Perm ι) :
    leviCivitaSymbol ⇑σ = (Equiv.Perm.sign σ : ℤ)

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_comp_swap
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol is antisymmetric under transposition of two of its indices:
precomposing with the swap of two distinct index positions negates it.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_comp_swap (g : ι → ι) {i j : ι} (hij : i ≠ j) :
    leviCivitaSymbol (g ∘ Equiv.swap i j) = - leviCivitaSymbol g

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_swap_comp
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol is antisymmetric under transposition of two index values:
postcomposing with the swap of two distinct values exchanges those two values wherever
they occur and negates it.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_swap_comp (g : ι → ι) {i j : ι} (hij : i ≠ j) :
    leviCivitaSymbol (Equiv.swap i j ∘ g) = - leviCivitaSymbol g

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_of_eq
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol vanishes on a repeated index: if two distinct index positions
`i ≠ j` carry the same value, the symbol is zero.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_of_eq {g : ι → ι} {i j : ι} (hij : i ≠ j) (h : g i = g j) :
    leviCivitaSymbol g = 0

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_of_not_injective
declarations.doc: The Levi-Civita symbol vanishes on maps which are not injective.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_of_not_injective {g : ι → ι} (h : ¬ Function.Injective g) :
    leviCivitaSymbol g = 0

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_iff
declarations.doc:
The Levi-Civita symbol vanishes exactly on maps with a repeated index, i.e. on maps
which are not injective.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_eq_zero_iff {g : ι → ι} :
    leviCivitaSymbol g = 0 ↔ ¬ Function.Injective g

declarations.name: leviCivitaSymbol_eq_prod_prod_Ioi
declarations.doc:
On `Fin n` the Levi-Civita symbol is the product over pairs `i < j` of the sign of
`g j - g i`. Unlike the determinant defining `leviCivitaSymbol`, this product is cheap to
evaluate, e.g. by `decide`.
declarations.statement:
lemma leviCivitaSymbol_eq_prod_prod_Ioi {n : ℕ} (g : Fin n → Fin n) :
    leviCivitaSymbol g =
      ∏ i, ∏ j ∈ Finset.Ioi i, (if g i < g j then 1 else if g i = g j then 0 else -1)

modules.title: The conjugate module
modules.doc:
Over a commutative star-ring `k`, the *conjugate module* `ConjModule M` of a `k`-module `M` is the
same additive group with the scalar action twisted by conjugation: `r • v := star r • v`. It turns a
sesquilinear pairing into a bilinear one: a map conjugate-linear in a slot `M` is linear in the slot
`ConjModule M`.

`ConjModule M` is a type synonym carrying a fresh `Module k` instance (`Module.compHom` along
`starRingEnd k`), so the twisted action does not leak onto `M` and vice versa. The canonical
conjugate-linear identity `conjEquiv : M ≃ₛₗ[starRingEnd k] ConjModule M`, the involution
`ConjModule (ConjModule M) ≃ₗ[k] M`, and the transported basis `Basis.conj` are provided.

## Key results

- `ConjModule` : the conjugate-module type synonym, with its twisted `Module` instance.
- `conjEquiv` : the canonical conjugate-linear equivalence `M ≃ₛₗ[starRingEnd k] ConjModule M`.
- `ConjModule.involution` : the involution `ConjModule (ConjModule M) ≃ₗ[k] M`.
- `Basis.conj` : a basis of `M` transported to a basis of `ConjModule M` (coordinates by `star`).

declarations.name: ConjModule
declarations.doc:
The conjugate module of `M`: the same additive group with the scalar action twisted by
conjugation, `r • v = star r • v`. A type synonym so the twisted action stays off `M`.
declarations.statement: def ConjModule (M : Type*)
instance : AddCommGroup (ConjModule M)

declarations.name: ConjModule.instModule
declarations.doc:
The twisted action `r • v = star r • v`, obtained by restricting scalars along the
conjugation ring endomorphism `starRingEnd k`.
declarations.statement: instance instModule : Module k (ConjModule M)

declarations.name: conjEquiv
declarations.doc:
The canonical conjugate-linear equivalence `M ≃ₛₗ[starRingEnd k] ConjModule M`, the identity on
the underlying additive group.
declarations.statement: def conjEquiv : M ≃ₛₗ[starRingEnd k] ConjModule M

declarations.name: ConjModule.involution
declarations.doc:
Conjugating twice returns the original module: the `k`-linear isomorphism
`ConjModule (ConjModule M) ≃ₗ[k] M`. It is `k`-linear, not merely semilinear, because
`starRingEnd k` composed with itself is the identity.
declarations.statement: def involution : ConjModule (ConjModule M) ≃ₗ[k] M

declarations.name: ConjModule.starFinsupp
declarations.doc: Coordinate-wise conjugation on `ι →₀ k`, a conjugate-linear self-equivalence.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def starFinsupp : (ι →₀ k) ≃ₛₗ[starRingEnd k] (ι →₀ k)

declarations.name: Basis.conj
declarations.doc:
A basis of `M` transported to a basis of `ConjModule M`: the same basis vectors, with
coordinates conjugated (`(Basis.conj b).repr v = star ∘ b.repr v`).
declarations.statement: noncomputable def _root_.Basis.conj (b : Basis ι k M) : Basis ι k (ConjModule M)

declarations.name: Basis.conj_repr_apply
declarations.doc: Coordinates in `Basis.conj b` are the `star` of the coordinates in `b`.
declarations.statement:
lemma _root_.Basis.conj_repr_apply (b : Basis ι k M) (v : ConjModule M) (i : ι) :
    (Basis.conj b).repr v i = star (b.repr ((conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M)).symm v) i)

declarations.name: Basis.conj_apply
declarations.doc: The basis vectors of `Basis.conj b` are those of `b`, viewed through `conjEquiv`.
declarations.statement:
lemma _root_.Basis.conj_apply (b : Basis ι k M) (i : ι) :
    Basis.conj b i = conjEquiv (k := k) (M := M) (b i)

modules.title: The cross product of three-dimensional vectors
modules.doc:
Identities for the cross product `⨯₃` on `Fin 3 → ℝ`, beyond those already in Mathlib, used in the
formalisation of rigid-body dynamics.

declarations.name: Matrix.cross_cross_self_apply
declarations.doc:
The component form of the triple cross product `v ⨯₃ (w ⨯₃ v)`: by the `bac−cab` identity its
`i`-th entry is `|v|² wᵢ − (v · w) vᵢ`, written with the explicit component sums `∑ k, (v k)²` and
`∑ j, v j * w j`.
declarations.statement:
lemma cross_cross_self_apply (v w : Fin 3 → ℝ) (i : Fin 3) :
    (v ⨯₃ (w ⨯₃ v)) i = (∑ k, (v k) ^ 2) * w i - (∑ j, v j * w j) * v i

declarations.name: Matrix.dotProduct_cross_cross_self
declarations.doc:
Contracting `w` with the triple cross product `v ⨯₃ (w ⨯₃ v)` gives `(w ⨯₃ v) ⬝ᵥ (w ⨯₃ v)`
(over `ℝ`, the squared length `|w × v|²`), by two cyclic permutations of the scalar triple
product.
declarations.statement:
lemma dotProduct_cross_cross_self {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (v w : Fin 3 → R) :
    w ⬝ᵥ (v ⨯₃ (w ⨯₃ v)) = (w ⨯₃ v) ⬝ᵥ (w ⨯₃ v)

declarations.name: Matrix.contDiff_cross_dotProduct_cross
declarations.doc:
The squared length `(ω ⨯₃ v) ⬝ᵥ (ω ⨯₃ v)` of the cross product with a fixed vector `ω` is a
smooth function of `v`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contDiff_cross_dotProduct_cross (ω : Fin 3 → ℝ) :
    ContDiff ℝ ⊤ fun v : Fin 3 → ℝ => (ω ⨯₃ v) ⬝ᵥ (ω ⨯₃ v)

modules.title: The hat map on three-dimensional vectors
modules.doc:
The hat map sends a vector `ω : Fin 3 → ℝ` to the skew-symmetric matrix `[ω]ₓ` characterised by
`[ω]ₓ *ᵥ v = ω ⨯₃ v`. It realises the correspondence between `ℝ³` and the skew-symmetric `3 × 3`
matrices (the Lie algebra `𝖘𝖔(3)`), and underlies the angular velocity of a rigid body.
The vee map only selects matrix entries and is defined for arbitrary coefficient types,
including operator-valued matrices.

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductMatrix
declarations.doc:
The hat map `[ω]ₓ`: the skew-symmetric `3 × 3` matrix acting as the cross product with `ω`,
i.e. `[ω]ₓ *ᵥ v = ω ⨯₃ v`.
declarations.statement: def crossProductMatrix (ω : Fin 3 → ℝ) : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℝ

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductMatrix_mulVec
declarations.doc: The hat matrix acts on a vector as the cross product.
declarations.statement:
lemma crossProductMatrix_mulVec (ω v : Fin 3 → ℝ) :
    crossProductMatrix ω *ᵥ v = ω ⨯₃ v

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductMatrix_transpose
declarations.doc: The hat map produces skew-symmetric matrices.
declarations.statement:
lemma crossProductMatrix_transpose (ω : Fin 3 → ℝ) :
    (crossProductMatrix ω)ᵀ = - crossProductMatrix ω

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductVee
declarations.doc:
The vee map: reads the vector off a `3 × 3` matrix with arbitrary coefficients.
For real coefficients, it is a left inverse of the hat map.
declarations.statement: def crossProductVee {α : Type*} (A : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) α) : Fin 3 → α

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductVee_crossProductMatrix
declarations.doc: The vee map is a left inverse of the hat map.
declarations.statement:
lemma crossProductVee_crossProductMatrix (ω : Fin 3 → ℝ) :
    crossProductVee (crossProductMatrix ω) = ω

declarations.name: Matrix.crossProductMatrix_crossProductVee
declarations.doc:
On skew-symmetric matrices the hat map is also a right inverse of the vee map: if `Aᵀ = -A`
then `[Aᵛ]ₓ = A`. Together with `crossProductVee_crossProductMatrix` this identifies `ℝ³` with the
skew-symmetric `3 × 3` matrices `𝖘𝖔(3)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma crossProductMatrix_crossProductVee {A : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℝ} (hA : Aᵀ = -A) :
    crossProductMatrix (crossProductVee A) = A

modules.title: The complete elliptic integral of the first kind
modules.doc:
This file may eventually be upstreamed to Mathlib.

## i. Overview

Legendre's complete elliptic integral of the first kind is, in the parameter convention,

`K(m) = ∫ φ in 0..π/2, (1 - m sin² φ) ^ (-1/2)`

(Abramowitz & Stegun 17.3.1). The physics literature more often uses the modulus convention and
writes `K(k)`, as Landau & Lifshitz do, for what is here `completeEllipticK (k ^ 2)`; the two
conventions are related by `m = k²`. Mathlib knows the Weierstrass elliptic function `℘`
(`PeriodPair.weierstrassP`) but has no Legendre-form elliptic integrals; this file defines the
complete integral of the first kind and develops its basic theory on the domain `m < 1`, where
the radicand `1 - m sin² φ` is positive and the integrand continuous.

The integral enters physics wherever a period or a potential is computed exactly rather than in a
small-parameter expansion. Physlib's use of it so far is the simple pendulum: released from rest
at amplitude `θ₀`, the pendulum has period `4 √(ℓ / g) K(sin² (θ₀ / 2))` (Landau & Lifshitz §11,
Problem 1), the consumer being `Physlib.ClassicalMechanics.Pendulum.SimplePendulum.PeriodFormula`.
More broadly, the complete integrals of the first and second kind give the magnetic field of a
circular current loop and the potential of a uniformly charged ring, and the second kind, `E`,
gives the arc length of an ellipse. This file defines `K` so that such results can be stated.

For `m ≥ 1` the definition still elaborates, but its value is not Legendre's. At `m = 1` the
integrand is `1 / cos φ`, which is not interval integrable on `[0, π/2]`, so the integral is `0`
by `intervalIntegral.integral_undef`, whereas `K(1) = ∞`. For `m > 1` the radicand is negative on
`(arcsin (1/√m), π/2]`, where the real power at exponent `-(1/2)` of a negative base vanishes
(`Real.rpow_def_of_neg` supplies the factor `cos (-(1 / 2) * π) = 0`), so the Lean value is the
finite positive integral over `[0, arcsin (1/√m)]`; by the reciprocal-modulus transformation this
is `K(1/m) / √m`, the real part of the complex Legendre integral (DLMF §19.7(ii)) — not proved
here. Every lemma of this file about a general parameter therefore carries its domain hypothesis
`m < 1` explicitly.

## ii. Key results

- `completeEllipticK` : the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, as a function of
  the parameter `m`.
- `completeEllipticK_zero` : `K 0 = π / 2`.
- `completeEllipticK_pos` : for `m < 1` the integral is positive.
- `completeEllipticK_mono` : for `m₁ ≤ m₂ < 1`, `K m₁ ≤ K m₂`.
- `completeEllipticK_strictMono` : for `m₁ < m₂ < 1`, `K m₁ < K m₂`.
- `pi_div_two_le_completeEllipticK` : for `0 ≤ m < 1`, `π / 2 ≤ K m`.
- `completeEllipticK_le` : for `0 ≤ m < 1`, `K m ≤ π / 2 * (1 - m) ^ (-1/2)`.
- `continuousOn_completeEllipticK` : `K` is continuous on `(-∞, 1)`.
- `continuousAt_completeEllipticK` : `K` is continuous at every `m < 1`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Definition and the integrand
- B. Value at zero and positivity
- C. Monotonicity and bounds in the parameter
- D. Continuity on the domain

## iv. References

* M. Abramowitz, I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions, §17.3 (the parameter convention,
  17.3.1). [ref: abramowitz_stegun_1964]
* NIST DLMF §19.7(ii) (the reciprocal-modulus transformation). [ref: nist_dlmf]
* Landau & Lifshitz, Mechanics, 3rd ed., §11, Problem 1 (the pendulum period as `K(k)`, modulus
  convention). [ref: landau_mechanics]

sections.text:
## A. Definition and the integrand

The integral is defined for every real parameter `m`; on the domain `m < 1` the radicand is
positive, so the integrand is continuous and interval integrable.

## B. Value at zero and positivity

At `m = 0` the integrand is the constant `1` and the integral is elementary; for `m < 1` the
integral is positive, being the integral of a positive continuous function.

## C. Monotonicity and bounds in the parameter

For fixed `φ` the radicand `1 - m sin² φ` decreases in `m`, so the integrand, a negative power of
the radicand, increases in `m` on the domain; integrating the pointwise inequality over
`[0, π/2]` gives monotonicity of `K`, and since the inequality is strict at `φ = π/2` the
monotonicity is strict. Together with `K 0 = π / 2` this bounds `K` below on `[0, 1)`; bounding
the radicand below by `1 - m` bounds `K` above by `π / 2 * (1 - m) ^ (-1/2)` there.

## D. Continuity on the domain

The integrand is jointly continuous in `(m, φ)` on `(-∞, 1) × ℝ`, where the radicand is
positive, but not on all of `ℝ × ℝ`. Restricting the parameter to the subtype `Set.Iio 1` makes
the joint continuity global, so Mathlib's continuity of a parametric interval integral with
fixed endpoints (`intervalIntegral.continuous_parametric_intervalIntegral_of_continuous'`)
applies and gives continuity of `K` on the domain. Continuity at each point `m < 1` follows,
`(-∞, 1)` being a neighbourhood of `m`.

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK
declarations.doc:
The complete elliptic integral of the first kind in the parameter convention,
`K(m) = ∫ φ in 0..π/2, (1 - m sin² φ) ^ (-1/2)`. The physics literature often writes `K(k)`
with `m = k²`. The integrand is written as a real power rather than `1 / √(…)` so that
continuity, positivity and monotonicity in `m` come from the `rpow` API (`Continuous.rpow_const`,
`Real.rpow_pos_of_pos`, `Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_nonpos`); the two forms agree by
`Real.sqrt_eq_rpow` and `Real.rpow_neg`. For `m ≥ 1` see the module docstring.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def completeEllipticK (m : ℝ) : ℝ

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_def
declarations.doc:
Unfolding lemma: `completeEllipticK m` is the interval integral of its integrand over
`[0, π/2]`.
declarations.statement:
lemma completeEllipticK_def (m : ℝ) :
    completeEllipticK m = ∫ φ in (0 : ℝ)..π / 2, (1 - m * sin φ ^ 2) ^ (-(1 / 2 : ℝ))

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_radicand_pos
declarations.doc:
For `m < 1` the radicand `1 - m sin² φ` of the integrand of `completeEllipticK m` is
positive at every angle `φ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma completeEllipticK_radicand_pos {m : ℝ} (hm : m < 1) (φ : ℝ) :
    0 < 1 - m * sin φ ^ 2

declarations.name: Real.continuous_completeEllipticK_integrand
declarations.doc:
For `m < 1` the integrand of `completeEllipticK m` is continuous, the real power being
taken at a positive base.
declarations.statement:
lemma continuous_completeEllipticK_integrand {m : ℝ} (hm : m < 1) :
    Continuous fun φ : ℝ => (1 - m * sin φ ^ 2) ^ (-(1 / 2 : ℝ))

declarations.name: Real.intervalIntegrable_completeEllipticK_integrand
declarations.doc: For `m < 1` the integrand of `completeEllipticK m` is interval integrable on `[0, π/2]`.
declarations.statement:
lemma intervalIntegrable_completeEllipticK_integrand {m : ℝ} (hm : m < 1) :
    IntervalIntegrable (fun φ : ℝ => (1 - m * sin φ ^ 2) ^ (-(1 / 2 : ℝ))) volume 0 (π / 2)

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_zero
declarations.doc: `K 0 = π / 2`: at parameter zero the integrand of `completeEllipticK` is the constant `1`.
declarations.statement: lemma completeEllipticK_zero : completeEllipticK 0 = π / 2

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_pos
declarations.doc: For `m < 1` the complete elliptic integral `completeEllipticK m` is positive.
declarations.statement: lemma completeEllipticK_pos {m : ℝ} (hm : m < 1) : 0 < completeEllipticK m

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_mono
declarations.doc:
`completeEllipticK` is monotone on its domain: for `m₁ ≤ m₂ < 1`, `K m₁ ≤ K m₂`. The
integrand is pointwise monotone in the parameter, the radicand being positive for both
parameters.
declarations.statement:
lemma completeEllipticK_mono {m₁ m₂ : ℝ} (h12 : m₁ ≤ m₂) (h2 : m₂ < 1) :
    completeEllipticK m₁ ≤ completeEllipticK m₂

declarations.name: Real.monotoneOn_completeEllipticK
declarations.doc: `completeEllipticK` is monotone on its domain `(-∞, 1)`, as a `MonotoneOn` statement.
declarations.statement: lemma monotoneOn_completeEllipticK : MonotoneOn completeEllipticK (Set.Iio 1)

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_strictMono
declarations.doc:
`completeEllipticK` is strictly monotone on its domain: for `m₁ < m₂ < 1`, `K m₁ < K m₂`.
The pointwise inequality between the integrands is strict at `φ = π / 2`, where `sin² φ = 1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma completeEllipticK_strictMono {m₁ m₂ : ℝ} (h12 : m₁ < m₂) (h2 : m₂ < 1) :
    completeEllipticK m₁ < completeEllipticK m₂

declarations.name: Real.strictMonoOn_completeEllipticK
declarations.doc: `completeEllipticK` is strictly increasing on `(-∞, 1)`, as a bundled `StrictMonoOn`.
declarations.statement: lemma strictMonoOn_completeEllipticK : StrictMonoOn completeEllipticK (Set.Iio 1)

declarations.name: Real.pi_div_two_le_completeEllipticK
declarations.doc:
For `0 ≤ m < 1` the complete elliptic integral `completeEllipticK m` is at least its value
`π / 2` at `m = 0`.
declarations.statement:
lemma pi_div_two_le_completeEllipticK {m : ℝ} (hm0 : 0 ≤ m) (hm1 : m < 1) :
    π / 2 ≤ completeEllipticK m

declarations.name: Real.completeEllipticK_le
declarations.doc:
For `0 ≤ m < 1` the complete elliptic integral `completeEllipticK m` is at most
`π / 2 * (1 - m) ^ (-1/2)`: the radicand is at least `1 - m`, `sin² φ` being at most `1`, so the
integrand is at most the constant `(1 - m) ^ (-1/2)`. With `pi_div_two_le_completeEllipticK` this
sandwiches `K` on `[0, 1)`; for the pendulum, where `m = sin² (θ₀ / 2)`, it bounds the period by
`T ≤ 2π √(ℓ / g) / cos (θ₀ / 2)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma completeEllipticK_le {m : ℝ} (hm0 : 0 ≤ m) (hm1 : m < 1) :
    completeEllipticK m ≤ π / 2 * (1 - m) ^ (-(1 / 2 : ℝ))

declarations.name: Real.continuousOn_completeEllipticK
declarations.doc: `completeEllipticK` is continuous on its domain `(-∞, 1)`.
declarations.statement: lemma continuousOn_completeEllipticK : ContinuousOn completeEllipticK (Set.Iio 1)

declarations.name: Real.continuousAt_completeEllipticK
declarations.doc:
`completeEllipticK` is continuous at every point `m < 1` of its domain, `(-∞, 1)` being a
neighbourhood of `m`.
declarations.statement: lemma continuousAt_completeEllipticK {m : ℝ} (hm : m < 1) : ContinuousAt completeEllipticK m

declarations.name: Real.continuousAt_completeEllipticK_zero
declarations.doc: `completeEllipticK` is continuous at `m = 0`, an interior point of its domain `(-∞, 1)`.
declarations.statement: lemma continuousAt_completeEllipticK_zero : ContinuousAt completeEllipticK 0

modules.title: Physicist's Hermite Polynomials
modules.doc:
This file may eventually be upstreamed to Mathlib.

## i. Overview

The physicist's Hermite polynomials are a family of orthogonal polynomials defined by the recursion
$H_0(x) = 1$ and $H_{n+1}(x) = 2x\,H_n(x) - H_n'(x)$.
These are a rescaling of the so-called probabalist's Hermite polynomials (`Polynomial.hermite`)
and, up to numerical factors, satisfy all of the same properties.

## ii. Key results

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Recursive definition
- B. Coefficients & degree
- C. Iterated derivatives
- D. As functions `ℝ → ℝ`
  - D.1. Recursion
  - D.2. Parity
  - D.3. Differentiability
  - D.4. Temperate growth
- E. Relationship to Gaussians

## iv. References

* None.

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite
declarations.doc:
The physicist's Hermite polynomials are defined as polynomials over `ℤ` in `X` recursively
with `physHermite 0 = 1` and

`physHermite (n + 1) = 2 • X * physHermite n - derivative (physHermite n)`.

This polynomial will often be cast as a function `ℝ → ℝ` by evaluating the polynomial at `X`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def physHermite : ℕ → Polynomial ℤ

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ
declarations.doc: The defining recursion `physHermite (n + 1) = (2x - d/dx) (physHermite n)`.
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ (n : ℕ) :
    physHermite (n + 1) = 2 • X * physHermite n - derivative (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_eq_iterate
declarations.doc: The Rodrigues formula `physHermite n = (2x - d/dx)ⁿ 1`.
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_eq_iterate (n : ℕ) :
    physHermite n = (fun p => 2 * X * p - derivative p)^[n] 1

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_zero
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_zero : physHermite 0 = C 1

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_one
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_one : physHermite 1 = 2 * X

declarations.name: Polynomial.derivative_physHermite_succ
declarations.statement:
lemma derivative_physHermite_succ : (n : ℕ) →
    derivative (physHermite (n + 1)) = 2 * (n + 1) • physHermite n

declarations.name: Polynomial.derivative_physHermite
declarations.statement:
lemma derivative_physHermite : (n : ℕ) →
    derivative (physHermite n) = 2 * n • physHermite (n - 1)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ'
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ' (n : ℕ) :
    physHermite (n + 1) = 2 • X * physHermite n - 2 * n • physHermite (n - 1)

declarations.name: Polynomial.coeff_physHermite_succ_zero
declarations.statement:
lemma coeff_physHermite_succ_zero (n : ℕ) :
    coeff (physHermite (n + 1)) 0 = - coeff (physHermite n) 1

declarations.name: Polynomial.coeff_physHermite_succ_succ
declarations.statement:
lemma coeff_physHermite_succ_succ (n k : ℕ) : coeff (physHermite (n + 1)) (k + 1) =
    2 * coeff (physHermite n) k - (k + 2) * coeff (physHermite n) (k + 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.coeff_physHermite_of_lt
declarations.statement: lemma coeff_physHermite_of_lt {n k : ℕ} (hnk : n < k) : coeff (physHermite n) k = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.coeff_physHermite_self
declarations.statement: lemma coeff_physHermite_self (n : ℕ) : coeff (physHermite n) n = 2 ^ n

declarations.name: Polynomial.degree_physHermite
declarations.statement: lemma degree_physHermite (n : ℕ) : degree (physHermite n) = n

declarations.name: Polynomial.natDegree_physHermite
declarations.statement: lemma natDegree_physHermite (n : ℕ) : (physHermite n).natDegree = n

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_leadingCoeff
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_leadingCoeff (n : ℕ) : (physHermite n).leadingCoeff = 2 ^ n

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_ne_zero
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_ne_zero (n : ℕ) : physHermite n ≠ 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.iterate_derivative_physHermite_of_gt
declarations.statement:
lemma iterate_derivative_physHermite_of_gt {n m : ℕ} (h : n < m) :
    derivative^[m] (physHermite n) = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.iterate_derivative_physHermite_self
declarations.statement:
lemma iterate_derivative_physHermite_self (n : ℕ) :
    derivative^[n] (physHermite n) = C (n ! * 2 ^ n : ℤ)

declarations.name: Polynomial.realEval
declarations.doc: Cast an integer polynomial to a function `ℝ → ℝ` by evaluation of the indeterminant.
declarations.statement: noncomputable abbrev realEval (p : Polynomial ℤ) : ℝ → ℝ
noncomputable instance : CoeFun (Polynomial ℤ) (fun _ ↦ ℝ → ℝ)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_zero_coe
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_zero_coe : (physHermite 0 : ℝ → ℝ) = fun _ ↦ 1

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ_coe
declarations.doc: The defining recursion for `physHermite` as functions `ℝ → ℝ` (c.f. `physHermite_succ`).
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ_coe (n : ℕ) :
    (physHermite (n + 1) : ℝ → ℝ) =
      2 • (fun x => x) * (physHermite n : ℝ → ℝ) - deriv (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ_apply
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ_apply (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    physHermite (n + 1) x = 2 * x * physHermite n x - deriv (physHermite n) x

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ_coe'
declarations.doc: The two-term recursion for `physHermite` as functions `ℝ → ℝ` (c.f. `physHermite_succ'`).
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ_coe' (n : ℕ) :
    (physHermite (n + 1) : ℝ → ℝ) =
      2 • (fun x => x) * (physHermite n : ℝ → ℝ) - (2 * n) • (physHermite (n - 1) : ℝ → ℝ)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_succ_apply'
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_succ_apply' (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    physHermite (n + 1) x = 2 * x * physHermite n x - 2 * n * physHermite (n - 1) x

declarations.name: Polynomial.deriv_physHermite
declarations.statement: lemma deriv_physHermite (n : ℕ) : deriv (physHermite n) = 2 * n * physHermite (n - 1)

declarations.name: Polynomial.iterate_deriv_physHermite_eq_iterate_derivative
declarations.statement:
lemma iterate_deriv_physHermite_eq_iterate_derivative (n m : ℕ) :
    deriv^[m] (physHermite n) = derivative^[m] (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.fderiv_physHermite
declarations.statement:
lemma fderiv_physHermite (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    fderiv ℝ (physHermite n) x = (1 : ℝ →L[ℝ] ℝ).smulRight (deriv (physHermite n) x)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_neg
declarations.doc: The `physHermite` polynomials are alternately even and odd.
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_neg (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) : physHermite n (-x) = (-1) ^ n * physHermite n x

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_even
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_even {n : ℕ} (hn : Even n) : Function.Even (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_odd
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_odd {n : ℕ} (hn : Odd n) : Function.Odd (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_differentiable
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_differentiable (n : ℕ) : Differentiable ℝ (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.deriv_physHermite_differentiable
declarations.statement: lemma deriv_physHermite_differentiable (n m : ℕ) : Differentiable ℝ (deriv^[m] (physHermite n))

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_continuous
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_continuous (n : ℕ) : Continuous (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_contDiff
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_contDiff (n : ℕ) (m : WithTop ℕ∞) : ContDiff ℝ m (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_hasTemperateGrowth
declarations.statement: lemma physHermite_hasTemperateGrowth (n : ℕ) : HasTemperateGrowth (physHermite n)

declarations.name: Polynomial.deriv_gaussian_eq_physHermite_mul_gaussian
declarations.statement:
lemma deriv_gaussian_eq_physHermite_mul_gaussian (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    deriv^[n] (fun y => Real.exp (- y ^ 2)) x =
    (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * physHermite n x * Real.exp (- x ^ 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_eq_deriv_gaussian
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_eq_deriv_gaussian (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    physHermite n x = (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * deriv^[n]
    (fun y => Real.exp (- y ^ 2)) x / Real.exp (- x ^ 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_eq_deriv_gaussian'
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_eq_deriv_gaussian' (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    physHermite n x = (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * deriv^[n] (fun y => Real.exp (- y ^ 2)) x *
    Real.exp (x ^ 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.guassian_integrable_polynomial_cons
declarations.statement:
lemma guassian_integrable_polynomial_cons {b c : ℝ} (hb : 0 < b) (P : Polynomial ℤ) :
    MeasureTheory.Integrable fun x : ℝ => (P.aeval (c * x)) * Real.exp (-b * x ^ 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.guassian_integrable_polynomial
declarations.statement:
lemma guassian_integrable_polynomial {b : ℝ} (hb : 0 < b) (P : Polynomial ℤ) :
    MeasureTheory.Integrable fun x : ℝ => (P.aeval x) * Real.exp (-b * x ^ 2)

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_gaussian_integrable
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_gaussian_integrable (n p m : ℕ) :
    MeasureTheory.Integrable (deriv^[m] (physHermite p) * deriv^[n] fun x => Real.exp (-x ^ 2))
    MeasureTheory.volume

declarations.name: Polynomial.integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv_exp
declarations.statement:
lemma integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv_exp (n m : ℕ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite m x) * Real.exp (-x ^ 2) =
    (-1 : ℝ) ^ m * ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * (deriv^[m] fun x => Real.exp (-x ^ 2)) x)

declarations.name: Polynomial.integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv_inductive
declarations.statement:
lemma integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv_inductive (n m : ℕ) :
    (p : ℕ) → (hpm : p ≤ m) →
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite m x) * Real.exp (- x ^ 2) =
    (-1 : ℝ) ^ (m - p) * ∫ x : ℝ, (deriv^[p] (physHermite n) x *
    (deriv^[m - p] fun x => Real.exp (-x ^ 2)) x)

declarations.name: Polynomial.integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv
declarations.statement:
lemma integral_physHermite_mul_physHermite_eq_integral_deriv (n m : ℕ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite m x) * Real.exp (- x ^ 2) =
    ∫ x : ℝ, (deriv^[m] (physHermite n) x * (Real.exp (-x ^ 2)))

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_orthogonal_lt
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_orthogonal_lt {n m : ℕ} (hnm : n < m) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite m x) * Real.exp (- x ^ 2) = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_orthogonal
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_orthogonal {n m : ℕ} (hnm : n ≠ m) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite m x) * Real.exp (- x ^ 2) = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_orthogonal_cons
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_orthogonal_cons {n m : ℕ} (hnm : n ≠ m) (c : ℝ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n (c * x) * physHermite m (c * x)) *
    Real.exp (- c ^ 2 * x ^ 2) = 0

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_norm
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_norm (n : ℕ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n x * physHermite n x) * Real.exp (- x ^ 2) =
    ↑n ! * 2 ^ n * √Real.pi

declarations.name: Polynomial.physHermite_norm_cons
declarations.statement:
lemma physHermite_norm_cons (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, (physHermite n (c * x) * physHermite n (c * x)) * Real.exp (- c ^ 2 * x ^ 2) =
    |c⁻¹| • (↑n ! * 2 ^ n * √Real.pi)

declarations.name: Polynomial.polynomial_mem_physHermite_span_induction
declarations.statement:
lemma polynomial_mem_physHermite_span_induction (P : Polynomial ℤ) : (n : ℕ) →
    (hn : P.natDegree = n) →
    (P : ℝ → ℝ) ∈ Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range (fun n => (physHermite n : ℝ → ℝ)))
  | 0, h => by
    obtain ⟨x, rfl⟩

declarations.name: Polynomial.polynomial_mem_physHermite_span
declarations.statement:
lemma polynomial_mem_physHermite_span (P : Polynomial ℤ) :
    (P : ℝ → ℝ) ∈ Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range (fun n => (physHermite n : ℝ → ℝ)))

declarations.name: Polynomial.cos_mem_physHermite_span_topologicalClosure
declarations.statement:
lemma cos_mem_physHermite_span_topologicalClosure (c : ℝ) :
    (fun (x : ℝ) => Real.cos (c * x)) ∈
    (Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range (fun n => (physHermite n : ℝ → ℝ)))).topologicalClosure

modules.title: Colors of tensor indices
modules.doc:
A color gives the kind of an index of a tensor and whether the index is up or down.

## i. Overview

A color `⟨κ, v⟩` is a kind of index `κ : K` and a variance `v`, `up` or `down`. For Lorentz
tensors there is one kind, `vec`. The vector index of `v^μ` has color `⟨vec, up⟩` and the
covector index of `w_μ` has color `⟨vec, down⟩`. Complex Lorentz tensors have three kinds, one
for each of the two types of Weyl spinor index and one for the vector index.

A tensor has one color per index. A species (`Species.lean`) gives each color a space, and a
tensor is an element of the tensor product of the spaces of its indices. Each index has a color
rather than a space, so that whether two indices can be contracted is an equation of colors,
`c j = (c i).dual`, which Lean checks by computation when the colors are known. When two colors
are equal only through a proof, vectors are moved between their spaces by `S.cast`
(`Species.lean`, §C).

The dual of `⟨κ, v⟩` is `⟨κ, v.dual⟩`, the same kind with the other variance. A contraction such
as `v^μ w_μ` pairs an index of color `c` with an index of color `c.dual`. `Color K` is a structure
rather than the product `K × Variance`, so that `c.dual` works as dot notation.

## ii. Key results

- `Variance` : the variance of an index, with `Variance.up`, `Variance.down` and
  `Variance.dual`.
- `Color` : a kind of index and a variance.
- `Color.dual` : the dual color, and `Color.dual_dual` : `c.dual.dual = c` by `rfl`.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Variance
- B. Colors

## iv. References

There are no known references for the material in this module.

sections.text:
## A. Variance

`Variance` is two booleans, and `dual` swaps them. So `c.dual.dual` is `c` by definition, also for
a variable color `c`, and the spaces `S.V c.dual.dual` and `S.V c` of a species are the same type.
## B. Colors

declarations.name: Tensor.Variance
declarations.doc: The variance of an index, up (contravariant, `v^μ`) or down (covariant, `w_μ`).
declarations.statement:
structure Variance where
  /-- Whether the index is up. -/
  isUp : Bool
  /-- Whether the index is down. -/
  isDown : Bool
  /-- An index is either up or down. -/
  ne : isUp ≠ isDown

declarations.name: Tensor.Variance.up
declarations.doc: An upper index, as in `v^μ`.
declarations.statement: abbrev up : Variance

declarations.name: Tensor.Variance.down
declarations.doc: A lower index, as in `w_μ`.
declarations.statement: abbrev down : Variance

declarations.name: Tensor.Variance.dual
declarations.doc:
The dual variance, exchanging up and down. It is an abbrev, so that `simp` and `rw` see
`c.dual.dual` as `c`.
declarations.statement: abbrev dual (v : Variance) : Variance

declarations.name: Tensor.Color
declarations.doc: A color `⟨κ, v⟩`, made of a kind of index `κ : K` and its variance `v`.
declarations.statement:
structure Color (K : Type) where
  /-- The kind of index, such as a Lorentz vector index or a left-handed Weyl spinor index. -/
  kind : K
  /-- Whether the index is up or down. -/
  variance : Variance

declarations.name: Tensor.Color.dual
declarations.doc: The dual color, with the same kind and the other variance.
declarations.statement: abbrev Color.dual {K : Type} (c : Color K) : Color K

declarations.name: Tensor.Color.dual_dual
declarations.doc: Taking the dual twice gives back the color.
declarations.statement: lemma Color.dual_dual {K : Type} (c : Color K) : c.dual.dual = c

modules.title: Tensor species
modules.doc:
A species gives each color of index a space, an action of the symmetry group and a basis. Its
tensors are built from these.

## i. Overview

A species `S : Species k G K basisIdx` over `k = ℝ` or `ℂ` (`RCLike k`) gives each color `c` a
`k`-vector space `S.V c`, a representation `S.rep c` of the group `G` on it, and a basis
`S.basis c`. A tensor of `S` with index colors `c₁, …, cₙ` is an element of `V c₁ ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ V cₙ`,
with the action of `G` on each factor.

For real Lorentz tensors in `1 + d` dimensions, `k = ℝ`, `G` is the Lorentz group, and there is
one kind `vec`, whose basis labels are `basisIdx vec = Fin 1 ⊕ Fin d`. The space of `⟨vec, up⟩`
is `Vector d`, the vectors with `1 + d` components, with the action `v^μ ↦ Λ^μ_ν v^ν` and the
standard basis `e_μ`. The space of `⟨vec, down⟩` is `CoVector d`, also with `1 + d` components,
with the action `w_μ ↦ w_ν (Λ⁻¹)^ν_μ` and the dual basis `e^μ`.

Each lower space is given by the species, not built as `Module.Dual` of the upper space, so that
a covector is an element of `CoVector d` itself rather than a linear form on `Vector d`. The bases
fix the contraction, which identifies `V c.dual` with the dual space of `V c`, and the condition on
the species makes this identification respect the group action:

- The contraction `S.contr c : V c ⊗ V c.dual → k` multiplies the components of its two arguments
  in the bases of `c` and `c.dual` and adds them up, `S.contr c (u ⊗ α) = ∑ μ, u^μ α_μ`. A basis
  vector has one component equal to `1` and the others `0`, so `S.contr c (e_μ ⊗ e^ν) = δ_μ^ν` and
  the two bases are dual. Every linear form on `V c` is `u ↦ u^μ α_μ` for exactly one `α`, with
  `α_μ` its value on `e_μ`, so the contraction identifies `V c.dual` with the dual space of `V c`
  (`isPerfPair_contr`).
- The condition on a species (`invariant`) says that the contraction is invariant,
  `(Λu)^μ (Λα)_μ = u^μ α_μ` for every `Λ : G`. Equivalently `u^μ (Λα)_μ = (Λ⁻¹u)^μ α_μ`
  (`contr_tmul_rep`), which is how `G` acts on linear forms on `V c`. So the identification
  respects the action, and `V c.dual` is the dual representation of `V c` (`dualEquiv`).

A repeated index is contracted, so `u^μ α_μ` is `S.contr c (u ⊗ α)`.

## ii. Key results

- `Species` : the data of a tensor species and the condition on it, and
  `Species.invariant_of_up` : the condition from the upper colors alone.
- `Species.contr` : the contraction `u^μ α_μ`, with `Species.contr_tmul_eq_sum_basis` : its
  formula in components, `Species.contr_basis` : the bases are dual, `Species.contr_tmul_symm` :
  it is symmetric, and `Species.contr_invariant` : it is invariant.
- `Species.isPerfPair_contr` : the contraction is a perfect pairing, `Species.ext_contr` : a
  vector of `V c.dual` is determined by its contractions, and `Species.dualEquiv` : `V c.dual` is
  the dual representation of `V c`.
- `Species.cast` : a vector moved along an equality of colors, with `Species.cast_rep`,
  `Species.basis_repr_cast`, `Species.contr_cast_tmul_cast` and
  `Species.contr_cast_tmul_cast_symm` : this keeps the action, the components and the
  contraction.

## iii. Table of contents

- A. Species
- B. The contraction
- C. Moving a vector along an equality of colors

## iv. References

There are no known references for the material in this module.

sections.text:
## A. Species

The basis of a color `c` is labelled by `basisIdx c.kind`, the values that an index of that kind
runs over. A color and its dual share labels, as `μ` in `v^μ` and `α_μ`. `basisIdx` is a
parameter of `Species`.

The condition is stated at every color, so that lemmas about a general color `c` use it directly.
At a lower color it is the condition at the upper color with the factors swapped, and
`invariant_of_up` proves it from the upper colors.

## B. The contraction

The contraction is not a field of `Species`. It is defined from the bases, as
`u ⊗ α ↦ ∑ μ, u^μ α_μ`, so the bases of `c` and `c.dual` are dual by definition
(`contr_basis`). Its invariance is the condition on the species. It is a perfect pairing in
Mathlib's sense, and `dualEquiv` identifies `V c.dual` with Mathlib's dual representation of
`V c`, so Mathlib's results on duals apply. When an invariant pairing for which the bases are
dual is already known, `Module.Basis.coordPairing_invariant` gives the condition.

## C. Moving a vector along an equality of colors

When two colors are equal by computation, as `c.dual.dual` and `c`, their spaces are the same
type. When they are equal only through a proof `p : a = a'`, Lean cannot use a vector of `S.V a`
where one of `S.V a'` is expected. This happens for a hypothesis such as `c i = a`, and for the
colors `c s` and `c s'` of two indices with `s = s'`. `S.cast p` moves the vector from `S.V a` to
`S.V a'` without changing it. The lemmas below say that `S.cast` keeps the group action, the
components and the contraction, so that proofs can remove it.

declarations.name: Tensor.Species
declarations.doc:
A tensor species gives each color `c` a space `V c`, a representation `rep c` of `G` on it and
a basis `basis c` labelled by `basisIdx c.kind`, so that a color and its dual share labels. Its one
condition, `invariant`, says that the coordinate pairing `u ⊗ α ↦ ∑ μ, u^μ α_μ` of the bases of
`c` and `c.dual` is invariant.
declarations.statement:
structure Species (k : Type) [RCLike k] (G : Type) [Group G] (K : Type)
    (basisIdx : K → Type) [∀ κ, Fintype (basisIdx κ)] [∀ κ, DecidableEq (basisIdx κ)] where
  /-- The vector space of a color. -/
  V : Color K → Type
  /-- The vector spaces are additive groups. -/
  [addCommGroup : ∀ c, AddCommGroup (V c)]
  /-- The vector spaces are modules over `k`. -/
  [module : ∀ c, Module k (V c)]
  /-- The representation of a color. -/
  rep : (c : Color K) → Representation k G (V c)
  /-- The basis of a color. -/
  basis : (c : Color K) → Module.Basis (basisIdx c.kind) k (V c)
  /-- The coordinate pairing `u ⊗ α ↦ ∑ μ, u^μ α_μ` of the bases of `c` and `c.dual` is
  invariant, `(Λu)^μ (Λα)_μ = u^μ α_μ`. -/
  invariant : ∀ c g x y, (basis c).coordPairing (basis c.dual) (rep c g x ⊗ₜ rep c.dual g y) =
    (basis c).coordPairing (basis c.dual) (x ⊗ₜ y)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.invariant_of_up
declarations.doc:
The condition `invariant` at every color from the condition at the upper colors. At a lower
color the pairing is the pairing at the dual, upper color with its factors swapped.
declarations.statement:
lemma invariant_of_up {V : Color K → Type} [∀ c, AddCommGroup (V c)] [∀ c, Module k (V c)]
    (rep : (c : Color K) → Representation k G (V c))
    (basis : (c : Color K) → Module.Basis (basisIdx c.kind) k (V c))
    (h : ∀ κ g x y, (basis ⟨κ, .up⟩).coordPairing (basis ⟨κ, .down⟩)
      (rep ⟨κ, .up⟩ g x ⊗ₜ rep ⟨κ, .down⟩ g y) =
        (basis ⟨κ, .up⟩).coordPairing (basis ⟨κ, .down⟩) (x ⊗ₜ y)) :
    ∀ c g x y, (basis c).coordPairing (basis c.dual) (rep c g x ⊗ₜ rep c.dual g y) =
      (basis c).coordPairing (basis c.dual) (x ⊗ₜ y)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.finiteDimensional
declarations.doc: The space of each color is finite-dimensional, since it has a finite basis.
declarations.statement:
instance finiteDimensional (S : Species k G K basisIdx) (c : Color K) :
    FiniteDimensional k (S.V c)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr
declarations.doc:
The invariant contraction `V c ⊗ V c.dual → k`, `u ⊗ α ↦ u^μ α_μ`, the coordinate pairing of
the bases. The vector of color `c` is the first factor.
declarations.statement:
noncomputable def contr (c : Color K) :
    ((S.rep c).tprod (S.rep c.dual)).IntertwiningMap (Representation.trivial k G k)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_basis
declarations.doc: The bases of a color and its dual are dual, `S.contr c (e_μ ⊗ e^ν) = δ_μ^ν`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_basis (c : Color K) (μ ν : basisIdx c.kind) :
    S.contr c (S.basis c μ ⊗ₜ S.basis c.dual ν) = if μ = ν then 1 else 0

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_tmul_eq_sum_basis
declarations.doc: The contraction in components, `S.contr c (u ⊗ α) = ∑ μ, u^μ α_μ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_tmul_eq_sum_basis (c : Color K) (x : S.V c) (y : S.V c.dual) :
    S.contr c (x ⊗ₜ y) = ∑ μ, (S.basis c).repr x μ * (S.basis c.dual).repr y μ

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_tmul_symm
declarations.doc:
The contraction is symmetric. `u^μ α_μ` at `c` is `α_μ u^μ` at `c.dual`, with the factors
swapped.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_tmul_symm (c : Color K) (x : S.V c) (y : S.V c.dual) :
    S.contr c (x ⊗ₜ[k] y) = S.contr c.dual (y ⊗ₜ[k] x)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.isPerfPair_contr
declarations.doc: The contraction is a perfect pairing, so it identifies `V c.dual` with the dual of `V c`.
declarations.statement:
instance isPerfPair_contr (c : Color K) :
    (TensorProduct.curry (S.contr c).toLinearMap).IsPerfPair

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.ext_contr
declarations.doc:
The contraction is nondegenerate in its second argument. Two vectors of `c.dual` with the
same contraction against every vector of `c` are equal.
declarations.statement:
lemma ext_contr {c : Color K} {α α' : S.V c.dual}
    (h : ∀ u, S.contr c (u ⊗ₜ α) = S.contr c (u ⊗ₜ α')) : α = α'

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_invariant
declarations.doc: The contraction is invariant, `(Λu)^μ (Λα)_μ = u^μ α_μ` for every `Λ : G`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_invariant (c : Color K) (g : G) (x : S.V c) (y : S.V c.dual) :
    S.contr c (S.rep c g x ⊗ₜ[k] S.rep c.dual g y) = S.contr c (x ⊗ₜ[k] y)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_tmul_rep
declarations.doc: Contracting `u` with `Λα` is contracting `Λ⁻¹u` with `α`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_tmul_rep (c : Color K) (g : G) (u : S.V c) (α : S.V c.dual) :
    S.contr c (u ⊗ₜ S.rep c.dual g α) = S.contr c (S.rep c g⁻¹ u ⊗ₜ α)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.dualEquiv
declarations.doc:
The space of `c.dual` is the dual representation of the space of `c`, a vector `α` read as the
linear form `u ↦ u^μ α_μ`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def dualEquiv (c : Color K) : (S.rep c.dual).Equiv (S.rep c).dual

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.dualEquiv_apply
declarations.doc: `dualEquiv c α` is the linear form `u ↦ u^μ α_μ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma dualEquiv_apply (c : Color K) (α : S.V c.dual) (u : S.V c) :
    S.dualEquiv c α u = S.contr c (u ⊗ₜ α)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.cast
declarations.doc:
Moving a vector along an equality of colors `a = a'`, Mathlib's `LinearEquiv.cast`, as an
equivalence of representations.
declarations.statement: protected def cast {a a' : Color K} (p : a = a') : (S.rep a).Equiv (S.rep a')

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.cast_apply
declarations.doc: `S.cast p` is Mathlib's `cast` of the vector.
declarations.statement:
lemma cast_apply {a a' : Color K} (p : a = a') (x : S.V a) :
    S.cast p x = cast (congrArg S.V p) x

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.cast_rep
declarations.doc: Moving a vector along an equality of colors `a = a'` commutes with the group action.
declarations.statement:
lemma cast_rep {a a' : Color K} (p : a = a') (g : G) (x : S.V a) :
    S.cast p (S.rep a g x) = S.rep a' g (S.cast p x)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.basis_repr_cast
declarations.doc:
Moving a vector along an equality of colors `a = b` keeps its components, with the label cast
back to a label at `a`.
declarations.statement:
lemma basis_repr_cast {a b : Color K} (p : a = b) (v : S.V a) (μ : basisIdx b.kind) :
    (S.basis b).repr (S.cast p v) μ =
      (S.basis a).repr v (cast (congrArg (basisIdx ∘ Color.kind) p.symm) μ)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.cast_apply_congr
declarations.doc:
For a family `f` of vectors on indices, moving `f s` to the color `b` is moving `f s'`, for
any index `s'` equal to `s`.
declarations.statement:
lemma cast_apply_congr {ι : Type} {d : ι → Color K} (f : Π s, S.V (d s)) {s s' : ι}
    (e : s = s') {b : Color K} (p : d s = b) : S.cast p (f s) = S.cast (e ▸ p) (f s')

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_cast_tmul_cast
declarations.doc: The contraction of two vectors does not depend on the colors they are moved to.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_cast_tmul_cast {d e a b : Color K} (x : S.V d) (y : S.V e) (p : d = a)
    (q : e = a.dual) (p' : d = b) (q' : e = b.dual) :
    S.contr a (S.cast p x ⊗ₜ S.cast q y) = S.contr b (S.cast p' x ⊗ₜ S.cast q' y)

declarations.name: Tensor.Species.contr_cast_tmul_cast_symm
declarations.doc:
The contraction of two vectors moved along equalities of colors is symmetric,
`u^μ α_μ = α_μ u^μ`.
declarations.statement:
lemma contr_cast_tmul_cast_symm {d e a b : Color K} (x : S.V d) (y : S.V e) (p : d = a)
    (q : e = a.dual) (p' : e = b) (q' : d = b.dual) :
    S.contr a (S.cast p x ⊗ₜ S.cast q y) = S.contr b (S.cast p' y ⊗ₜ S.cast q' x)

modules.title: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
modules.doc:
The key took in variational calculus is:
```
∀ h, ∫ x, f x * h x = 0 → f = 0
```
which allows use to go from reasoning about integrals to reasoning about functions.

## Overview of variational calculus

The variational calculus API in Physlib is designed to match and formalize the physicists intuition
of variational calculus. It is not designed to be a general API for variational calculus.

Within variational caclulus we are interested in function transformations, `F : (X → U) → (Y → V)`.
In physics this functional is often of the form `L : (Time → U) → Time → ℝ`,
which represents the Lagrangian of a system. We will use this to explain the formalization
within this API.

The action is nominally given by
$$S[u] = \int L(u, t) dt,$$
however it is convenient to
introduce another function `φ` and define the action as
$$S[u] = \int φ(t) L(u, t) dt.$$
In the end we will set `φ := fun _ => 1`.

We now consider $$\frac{\partial}{\partial s} S[u + s * \delta u]$$ at `s = 0`,
which is the variational derivative of `S` at `u` in the direction `δu`.
This is equal to
$$
\int φ(t) * \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial s} L(u + s * \delta u, t)\right|_{s = 0}dt
$$
Let us denote the function
$$
\delta u,\, t \mapsto \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial s} L(u + s * \delta u, t)\right|_{s = 0}
$$ as `Lᵤ : (Time → U) → (Time → ℝ)`.
Then the variational derivative is
$$\int φ (t) Lᵤ(δu, t) dt.$$

It may then be possible to find a function `Gᵤ : (Time → ℝ) → Time → U`
such that
$$
\int φ(t) Lᵤ(δu, t) dt = \int \langle Gᵤ(φ, t), δu(t)\rangle dt
$$
This is usually done by integration by parts.

We now set `φ := fun _ => 1` and get `grad u := Gᵤ (fun _ => 1)`, which is the
variational gradient at `u`. The Euler–Lagrange equations, for example, are then `grad u = 0`.

In our API, the relationship between
- `Lᵤ` and `Gᵤ` is captured by the `HasVarAdjoint`.
- `L` and `Gᵤ` by `HasVarAdjDeriv`.
- `L` and `grad u` by `HasVarGradientAt`.

In practice we assume that `L` has a certain locality property
`IsLocalizedFunctionTransform`, which allows us to work with functions
`φ` and `δu` which have compact support.

This API assumes that `U` is an inner-product space. This can be considered as the full
configuration space, or a local chart thereof.

## References

* https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/479953-Physlib/topic/Variational.20Calculus/with/529022834.

declarations.name: fundamental_theorem_of_variational_calculus'
declarations.doc:
A version of `fundamental_theorem_of_variational_calculus'` for `Continuous f`.
The proof uses assumption that source of `f` is finite-dimensional
inner-product space, so that a bump function with compact support exists via
`ContDiffBump.hasCompactSupport` from `Analysis.Calculus.BumpFunction.Basic`.

The proof is by contradiction, assume that there is `x₀` such that `f x₀ ≠ 0` then one construct
construct `g` test function *supported* on the neighborhood of `x₀` such that `⟪f x, g x⟫ ≥ 0`
and `⟪f x, g x⟫ > 0` on a neighborhood of x₀.

Using `Y` for the theorem below to make use of bump functions in InnerProductSpaces. `Y` is
a finite dimensional measurable space over `ℝ` with (standard) inner product.
declarations.statement:
lemma fundamental_theorem_of_variational_calculus' {f : Y → V}
    (μ : Measure Y) [IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ] [μ.IsOpenPosMeasure]
    [OpensMeasurableSpace Y]
    (hf : Continuous f) (hg : ∀ g, IsTestFunction g → ∫ x, ⟪f x, g x⟫_ℝ ∂μ = 0) :
    f = 0

declarations.name: fundamental_theorem_of_variational_calculus
declarations.statement:
lemma fundamental_theorem_of_variational_calculus {f : X → V}
    (μ : Measure X) [IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ] [μ.IsOpenPosMeasure]
    [OpensMeasurableSpace X]
    (hf : IsTestFunction f) (hg : ∀ g, IsTestFunction g → ∫ x, ⟪f x, g x⟫_ℝ ∂μ = 0) :
    f = 0

modules.title: Variational adjoint derivative
modules.doc:
Variational adjoint derivative of `F` at `u` is a generalization of `(fderiv ℝ F u).adjoint`
to function spaces. In particular, variational gradient is an analog of
`gradient F u := (fderiv ℝ F u).adjoint 1`.

The definition of `HasVarAdjDerivAt` is constructed exactly such that we can prove composition
theorem saying
```
  HasVarAdjDerivAt F F' (G u)) → HasVarAdjDerivAt G G' u →
    HasVarAdjDerivAt (F ∘ G) (G' ∘ F') u
```
This theorem is the main tool to mechanistically compute variational gradient.

declarations.name: HasVarAdjDerivAt
declarations.doc:
This is analogue of saying `F' = (fderiv ℝ F u).adjoint`.

This definition is useful as we can prove composition theorem for it and `HasVarGradient F grad u`
can be computed by `grad := F' (fun _ => 1)`.
declarations.statement:
structure HasVarAdjDerivAt (F : (X → U) → (Y → V)) (F' : (Y → V) → (X → U)) (u : X → U) : Prop
    where
  smooth_at : ContDiff ℝ ∞ u
  diff : ∀ (φ : ℝ → X → U), ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿φ →
    ContDiff ℝ ∞ (fun sx : ℝ×Y => F (φ sx.1) sx.2)
  linearize :
    ∀ (φ : ℝ → X → U), ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿φ →
      ∀ x,
        deriv (fun s' : ℝ => F (φ s') x) 0
        =
        deriv (fun s' : ℝ => F (fun x => φ 0 x + s' • deriv (φ · x) 0) x) 0
  adjoint : HasVarAdjoint (fun δu x => deriv (fun s : ℝ => F (fun x' => u x' + s • δu x') x) 0) F'

    (add : ∀ φ1 φ2 : X → U,
    ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ1 → ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ2 → F (φ1 + φ2) = F φ1 + F φ2)
    (smul : ∀ (c : ℝ) (φ : X → U), ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ → F (c • φ) = c • F φ)
    (deriv_comm : ∀ {φ : ℝ → X → U} (_ : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿φ) (x : X),
      deriv (fun s' => F (φ s') x) 0 = F (fun x' => deriv (fun x => φ x x') 0) x)

    (hφ : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿φ) (x : X) :

    (u : X → U) (smooth : ContDiff ℝ ∞ u)

    HasVarAdjoint (fun δu x => deriv (fun s : ℝ => F (fun x' => u x' + s • δu x') x) 0) F'

      ContDiff ℝ ∞ (fun sx : ℝ×X => F (φ sx.1) sx.2))

    (add : ∀ φ1 φ2 : X → U,
    ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ1 → ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ2 → F (φ1 + φ2) = F φ1 + F φ2)
    (smul : ∀ (c : ℝ) (φ : X → U), ContDiff ℝ ∞ φ → F (c • φ) = c • F φ)
    (deriv_comm : ∀ {φ : ℝ → X → U} (_ : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿φ) (x : X),
      deriv (fun s' => F (φ s') x) 0 = F (fun x' => deriv (fun x => φ x x') 0) x)

modules.title: Variational adjoint
modules.doc:
Definition of adjoint of linear function between function spaces. It is inspired by the definition
of distributional adjoint of linear maps between test functions as described here:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics) under 'Preliminaries: Transpose of a linear
operator' but we require that the adjoint is function between test functions too.

The key results are:
  - variational adjoint is unique on test functions
  - variational adjoint of identity is identity, `HasVarAdjoint.id`
  - variational adjoint of composition is composition of adjoint in reverse order,
    `HasVarAdjoint.comp`
  - variational adjoint of deriv is `- deriv`, `HasVarAdjoint.deriv`
  - variational adjoint of algebraic operations is algebraic operation of adjoints,
    `HasVarAdjoint.neg`, `HasVarAdjoint.add`, `HasVarAdjoint.sub`, `HasVarAdjoint.mul_left`,
    `HasVarAdjoint.mul_right`, `HasVarAdjoint.smul_left`, `HasVarAdjoint.smul_right`

declarations.name: HasVarAdjoint
declarations.doc:
Map `F` from `(X → U)` to `(X → V)` has a variational adjoint `F'` if it preserves
test functions and satisfies the adjoint relation `⟪F φ, ψ⟫ = ⟪φ, F' ψ⟫`for all test functions
`φ` and `ψ` for `⟪φ, ψ⟫ = ∫ x, ⟪φ x, ψ x⟫_ℝ ∂μ`.

The canonical example is the function `F = deriv` that has adjoint `F' = - deriv`.

This notion of adjoint allows us to do formally variational calculus as often encountered in physics
textbooks. In mathematical literature, the adjoint is often defined for unbounded operators, but
such formal treatment is unnecessarily complicated for physics applications.
declarations.statement:
structure HasVarAdjoint
    (F : (X → U) → (Y → V)) (F' : (Y → V) → (X → U)) where
  test_fun_preserving : ∀ φ, IsTestFunction φ → IsTestFunction (F φ)
  test_fun_preserving' : ∀ φ, IsTestFunction φ → IsTestFunction (F' φ)
  adjoint : ∀ φ ψ, IsTestFunction φ → IsTestFunction ψ →
    ∫ y, ⟪F φ y, ψ y⟫_ℝ = ∫ x, ⟪φ x, F' ψ x⟫_ℝ
  ext' : IsLocalizedFunctionTransform F'

modules.title: Variational gradient
modules.doc:
Definition of variational gradient that allows for formal treatment of variational calculus
as used in physics textbooks.

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt
declarations.doc:
Function `grad` is variational gradient of functional `S` at point `u`.

This formalizes the notion of variational gradient `δS/δu` of a functional `S` at a point `u`.

However, it is not defined for a functional `S : (X → U) → ℝ` but rather for the function
`S' : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)` which is related to the usual functional as `S u = ∫ x, S' (u x) x ∂μ`.
For example for action integral, `S u = ∫ t, L (u t) (deriv u t)` we have
`S' u t = L (u t) (deriv u t)`. Working with `S'` rather than with `S` allows us to ignore certain
technicalities with integrability.

Examples:

Euler-Lagrange equations:
```
δ/δx ∫ L(x,ẋ) dt = ∂L/∂ x - d/dt (∂L/∂ẋ)
```
can be expressed as
```
HasVarGradientAt
  (fun u t => L (u t) (deriv u t))
  (fun t =>
    deriv (L · (deriv u t)) ((u t))
    -
    deriv (fun t' => deriv (L (u t') ·) (deriv u t')) t)
  u
```

Laplace equation is variational gradient of Dirichlet energy:
```
δ/δu ∫ 1/2*‖∇u‖² = - Δu
```
can be expressed as
```
HasVarGradientAt
  (fun u t => 1/2 * deriv u t^2)
  (fun t => - deriv (deriv u) t)
  u
```
declarations.statement:
inductive HasVarGradientAt (F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)) (grad : X → U) (u : X → U) : Prop
  | intro (F') (hF' : HasVarAdjDerivAt F F' u) (hgrad : grad = F' (fun _ => 1))

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt.add
declarations.statement:
lemma HasVarGradientAt.add (F F' : (X → U) → (X → ℝ))
    {grad grad' : X → U} {u : X → U} [OpensMeasurableSpace X]
    [IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts (@volume X _)]
    (h : HasVarGradientAt F grad u) (h' : HasVarGradientAt F' grad' u) :
    HasVarGradientAt (F + F') (grad + grad') u

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt.sum
declarations.statement:
lemma HasVarGradientAt.sum {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] (F : ι → (X → U) → (X → ℝ))
    {grad : ι → X → U} {u : X → U} (hu : ContDiff ℝ ∞ u) [OpensMeasurableSpace X]
    [IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts (@volume X _)]
    (h : ∀ i, HasVarGradientAt (F i) (grad i) u) :
    HasVarGradientAt (fun v x => ∑ i, F i v x) (∑ i, grad i) u

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt.neg
varGradient
declarations.doc:
The variational gradient of a function `F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)` evaluated
at a function `u : X → U`.

This not defined defined for a functional `S : (X → U) → ℝ` but rather for the function
`F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)` which is the integrand of the functional `S u = ∫ x, F (u x) x ∂μ`.
For example for action integral, `S u = ∫ t, L (u t) (deriv u t)` we have
`S' u t = L (u t) (deriv u t)`.

On functions `F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)` which do not have a variational gradient,
this function is defined to give `0`.
declarations.statement: noncomputable def varGradient (F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)) (u : X → U) : X → U

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt.unique
declarations.statement:
lemma unique
    {S' : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)} {grad grad' : X → U} {u : X → U}
    (h : HasVarGradientAt S' grad u) (h' : HasVarGradientAt S' grad' u) :
    grad = grad'

declarations.name: HasVarGradientAt.varGradient
declarations.statement:
protected lemma varGradient
    (F : (X → U) → (X → ℝ)) (grad : X → U) (u : X → U)
    (hF : HasVarGradientAt F grad u) :
    varGradient F u = grad

modules.title: Fundamental lemma on an interval
modules.doc:
The fundamental lemma of variational calculus on `[a, b]`.

## i. Overview

A covector-valued `f` continuous on `[a, b]` with zero integral against every smooth `ψ`
supported in `(a, b)` vanishes. This is the step from a stationary action to the Euler-Lagrange
equations, see `LagrangianSystem.eulerLagrange_eq_zero_of_isCriticalPoint`.

## ii. Key results

- `eqOn_Icc_zero_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq_zero`: the fundamental lemma on `[a, b]`

## iii. Table of contents

- A. The fundamental lemma

## iv. References

* V. I. Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics. [ref: arnold_mechanics]
* L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, Mechanics. [ref: landau_mechanics]

sections.text: ## A. The fundamental lemma

declarations.name: eqOn_Icc_zero_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq_zero
declarations.doc:
If `f : ℝ → V →L[ℝ] ℝ` is continuous on `[a, b]` and `∫ x in a..b, f x (ψ x • v) = 0` for
every smooth `ψ` supported in `(a, b)` and every `v : V`, then `f = 0` on `[a, b]`.
declarations.statement:
lemma eqOn_Icc_zero_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq_zero {f : ℝ → V →L[ℝ] ℝ} {a b : ℝ}
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b)) (hab : a < b)
    (hint : ∀ ψ : ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ ∞ ψ → tsupport ψ ⊆ Ioo a b →
      ∀ v : V, ∫ x in a..b, f x (ψ x • v) = 0) :
    ∀ x ∈ Icc a b, f x = 0

modules.title: Localized function transforms
modules.doc:
In this module we define a locality property for function transforms, `F : (X → U) → (Y → V)`.
The locality property `IsLocalizedFunctionTransform`, says that for every compact
set `K` in `Y` there exists a compact set `L` of `X`, such that if `φ` and `φ'` are equal on `L`,
then `F φ` and `F φ'` are equal on `K`.

declarations.name: IsLocalizedFunctionTransform
declarations.doc:
Function transformation `F` is localizable if the values of the transformed function `F φ` on
some compact set `K` can depend only on the values of `φ` on some another compact set `L`.
declarations.statement: def IsLocalizedFunctionTransform (F : (X → U) → (Y → V)) : Prop
